entries.title: The Renters Take Providence
entries.summary: On September 9 the incumbent mayor of Providence, Rhode Island, Brett Smiley, lost his reelection bid to a twenty-seven-year-old democratic socialist named David Morales. entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
On September 9 the incumbent mayor of Providence, Rhode Island, Brett Smiley, lost his reelection bid to a twenty-seven-year-old democratic socialist named David Morales. It was the first time an incumbent mayor failed to win his party’s primary in the city’s history, and the latest in a wave of progressive victories over establishment Democrats that began with Zohran Mamdani last year.

Under the slogan “A Providence for All,” Morales emphasized the cost-of-living crisis, public education, protecting immigrants, and a Mr. Rogers-style neighborliness. He cut a whimsical figure on the campaign trail, in his signature bright blue suit and floral tie. In videos shot around the city, he shook hands with passersby as they recounted their struggles to pay rent, cover bus fare, and educate their children. The Smiley campaign spent more than $1.7 million, the lion’s share on television ad buys (much of it fear-mongering attacks on Morales for being soft on crime). The Morales campaign raised about $500,000, mobilized thousands of volunteers, and knocked 80,000 doors in a city of 190,000 people.

More than anything else, Morales ran on housing, which has become the animating issue in Rhode Island politics. When rents rose precipitously during the Covid-19 pandemic, Providence arguably felt the effects even more intensely than cities that had long been expensive, like San Francisco or nearby Boston. Between 2020 and 2024 the median rent increased more than 40 percent. In 2024 The Providence Journal reported that the city had seen the highest year-over-year rent increase in the country—16 percent. What was already a crisis for low-income Rhode Islanders became a problem for the middle class, too, as home values shot up all over town. More and more people entered homelessness for the first time.

The Providence left, including Morales, has spent the last six years arguing that the housing crisis epitomizes the inequality that defines our era. They have responded in part by organizing poor and working-class tenants to negotiate with their landlords for better conditions and more affordable rents. Smiley, meanwhile, sided with a political establishment that has catered to investors and wealthy transplants to Providence and blocked efforts to curtail landlords’ power over their tenants. In the eyes of many Rhode Islanders, he also came to represent the landlord class itself: although the Morales campaign almost never mentioned it on the campaign trail, it’s common knowledge in the state that Smiley owns three homes, including a modernist manse in the pricey beach community of Tiverton, and is married to the real estate tycoon Jim DeRentis.

This turned the mayoral race into a proxy for a broader contest between renters and the real estate industry over who would determine the city’s direction. The same themes were central to the campaigns of eight left-wing candidates for city council who ran alongside Morales—all of whom won their races, installing a progressive majority in City Hall. According to The Providence Journal, it was tenants who decided the election, with three renter-heavy neighborhoods likely delivering Morales’s victory.

A week after Morales won the primary, he celebrated his twenty-eighth birthday. He posted a photo on social media of a gathering at Charles Place, a subsidized housing development. Earlier in the summer, the tenants of that building formed a supermajority tenant union to demand that their landlord collectively bargain a new lease. In the photo, the presumptive mayor sat beaming in front of his cake, the members of the union—of his coalition—arrayed behind him.

Morales grew up in Soledad, California, where his mother raised him on her own. When we spoke after the primary, he remembered couch surfing when the family was between apartments, until they were able to secure a public housing unit when he was twelve years old. Diligent and driven from an early age, he graduated from the University of California, Irvine, as a teenager, and in 2019, at twenty, became the youngest person to complete Brown University’s public affairs master’s program.

The next year Morales challenged his state representative, Daniel McKiernan, who was running for a fourth term representing a working-class section of Providence. On the campaign trail he talked about housing, education, and the need to raise the minimum wage in Rhode Island, which at the time was $10.50 an hour, significantly lower than in neighboring states. Morales won, securing nearly 50 percent of the vote.

By the time he took office in 2021, everyone in Providence was talking about “the housing crisis.” There was a general sense that the moment’s defining issue had been met with an inept and inadequate response. Since 1991 all thirty-nine cities and towns in Rhode Island have been required to ensure that at least 10 percent of their housing stock meets affordability requirements, but as of last year only eight cities had reached the benchmark. Rhode Island ranks among the lowest in the nation for housing production. Activists covered the city in stickers reading “Freeze Rents, Not People,” the letters icy blue and snowcapped. More and more people stood on street corners and meridians with signs pleading for help.

Advertisement

For elected officials, the central question was what the government could or should do to address the problem. The state created its first-ever cabinet-level housing secretary position in 2022—a move that was intended to pave the way for a statewide housing plan, and which Morales supported—but in its first three years the department ran through as many directors. Meanwhile, establishment Democrats responded by trying to facilitate affordable housing production. Between 2022 and 2025, lawmakers in the state proposed historic bond measures alongside legislation that loosened regulations around accessory dwelling units, revised zoning laws and the state building code, and repurposed vacant buildings, among other measures. These policies promised more units and a more stable housing market in the future but didn’t ameliorate the struggle many Rhode Islanders faced writing their rent check every month. Of the fifty-two bills that leadership put forth in a four-year period, only one directly addressed tenant issues—a ban on rental application fees that had been introduced by one of Morales’s progressive colleagues in the statehouse, Cherie Cruz.

Smiley likewise responded in Providence by trying to spur developers to build housing. He eased zoning regulations, sped up permitting processes, and increased funding for new construction. In campaign literature this year, he claimed to have overseen the creation of thousands of new housing units across income levels during his term.* “I talked to people in the business community, construction and development people, along with nonprofit developers,” Smiley told me. “What we tried to do was do everything. It was our belief that there was no silver bullet.” In the most recent budget, Smiley also continued funding for legal services that provide eviction defense, as well as funding to enforce minimum housing standards, and proposed a $1 million fund that would provide up to $3,000 in emergency relief to people facing eviction or foreclosure. But although he acknowledged the crisis tenants were facing, he allocated far more resources to new development—through tax breaks and subsidies—than to tenant protections.

At the same time, a vision in which the public sector assumed more responsibility for the crisis was taking shape on Providence’s grassroots socialist left. One organization in particular, Reclaim Rhode Island, begun after Bernie Sanders’s 2020 presidential campaign, was increasingly focused on challenging the power of real estate developers, financial institutions, and landlords. Its first major foray into housing organizing was a 2022 campaign to create the country’s first state-level public developer. Modeled on efforts in Montgomery County, Maryland, and Seattle, Washington, such an institution would not only provide state-backed financing for building affordable housing, but also maintain public ownership—an alternative to the prevailing approach, which relies overwhelmingly on the private sector. The goal, Reclaim and its allies argue, is to build the kind of “social housing” constructed in Red Vienna in the 1930s: dense, thoughtfully designed apartment buildings that appeal to people at a range of income levels. Since 2022 the state has appropriated $20 million for public development, but the funds have ultimately been redirected to existing public housing authorities rather than put toward exploring a new model.

For Reclaim, the campaign went beyond the effort to build new units, as significant as that might be. “We are not ‘housing people’ who started a housing and tenant organization,” said Daniel Denvir, the group’s cofounder and current cochair (and the host of a popular left-wing podcast, The Dig). “We’re socialists who were exploring how to build power and decided upon housing as the way to do that.” To push the public developer model was to insist that the government should use public resources to reduce the power of the real estate industry and private financial institutions.

At the same time, Reclaim had started knocking on tenants’ doors. Nationwide, tenant organizing picked up steam during the Covid-19 pandemic; a few tenant union efforts had flared up in Providence but quickly fizzled out. Hoping to seed a broader movement of organized poor and working-class people, Reclaim pursued a strategy pioneered by the Connecticut Tenants Union and SEIU 1199 New England, in which tenants form a supermajority in a building and collectively bargain leases with their landlord.

The tenants of the first landlord Reclaim took on were living with floods, rodents, and malfunctioning toilets. Accustomed to being ignored, many were eager to talk to the organizers who showed up at their doors. “I was fighting all this on my own for the first, like, two years,” one woman—who had been trying in vain to get the landlord to fix her apartment’s exposed drywall, broken heaters, and cockroach infestation—told me when I reported on these efforts at the time. Within two years the group had helped organize the tenants of two corporate landlords who collectively owned more than four hundred units. But the project never coalesced into the statewide movement Reclaim envisioned. In both cases, the landlords retaliated, stoking fear among tenants, and novice organizers struggled to respond; the fledgling unions soon petered out. (They did result in legal action against the landlords; both cases are ongoing.)

Advertisement

Meanwhile, Morales had been working in the statehouse to advance tenant protection legislation. During his first two years in office, he introduced bills to limit rental application fees, cap rent increases, and replace lead pipes carrying water into people’s homes—but without a broad tenant movement behind them, and facing a well-funded landlord lobby, the bills never made it out of committee. (Morales did work on successful legislation that facilitated access to health care for pregnant people, lowered the price of insulin, and legalized cannabis, as well as a bill that required landlords to accept Section 8 housing vouchers, which preceded the leadership’s push to introduce housing packages.)

The attempts to empower tenants in their buildings and in the statehouse began to come together in late 2022. Reclaim was encountering an issue that often exemplifies landlord impunity in Rhode Island: childhood lead poisoning. Organizers met several families whose children had been exposed to lead paint, and at least one whose children were severely poisoned, despite state laws requiring landlords to safeguard tenants against such hazards. At around the same time, the attorney general in Rhode Island decided to prioritize enforcing lead laws and asked legislators to pass new protections. While Reclaim knocked doors, Morales and his progressive colleagues in the legislature (many of whom Reclaim and other left-wing organizations like the Rhode Island Working Families Party had helped to elect) introduced several bills to protect tenants from lead.

Reclaim and other housing advocacy groups backed the legislation and a bigger slate of pro-renter bills by turning out dozens of tenants to the statehouse for a rally. Morales spoke, as did Cruz (the two are among a small minority of lawmakers who are also renters). “We flooded the statehouse with over one hundred tenants in red shirts and delayed session from starting,” Morales remembered in a recent interview. “They made it very clear they had to pass tenant protections.”

In hearings over the next few months, fierce and coordinated opposition from landlords attempted to convey the opposite. One landlord wrote in a public comment that the rental registry law was “a gross, tyrannical step by the statewide government and an attack on a citizen’s privacy,” and “a blatant attack on those that are trying to provide housing.” Another threatened that he was “done in RI, because of your shenanigans, I am liquidating.” A third warned: “If you pass this, I’m going to evict every single tenant.”

Tenants also told their stories to lawmakers. One mom testified with a Ziploc bag of lead paint chips in her hand. Organizers from Reclaim had knocked on her door a few months earlier, and she was ready to speak out. “This is what falls off my walls every day, and this has lead,” she said at a hearing. “I have to live in fear of this right here falling off every day. And nothing gets done.” Less than two months later, the governor signed the lead safety measures into law.

Morales decided to primary Smiley in January 2025. At the beginning of the year, a polar vortex sent temperatures in Rhode Island into the teens. Homelessness outreach workers warned that many people faced spending the night outside, in tents. Since the pandemic, the state’s homelessness response system has been overwhelmed, leading to long waits for temporary shelter beds. Advocates called on Smiley to open an overnight emergency shelter for the duration of the cold snap, but he refused.

On the night of January 7, when the temperature outside was 17 degrees, two young, progressive city councilors, Miguel Sanchez and Justin Roias, decided to take action. Against the mayor’s orders, but with the blessing of the council president, they turned the city council chambers into a makeshift shelter for the night. At the time I covered housing in Rhode Island for the local NPR station. I showed up to find that they had worked with social service agencies to coordinate warm meals and a coat drive, and had placed a sign in front of the council chambers that read “Welcome, Warming Area / Bienvenido Área de calentamiento.”

Over the next few hours, dozens of people showed up to sleep on the benches in the council chamber. Many seemed tentative as they climbed up the marble stairs and passed through the heavy wooden doors. A team of legal observers stood by, and community members and other elected officials, including Morales, arrived to help. Donations of blankets, food, and hot chocolate poured in from the community. About thirty homeless people ultimately spent the night. So did Morales, who recalled in a recent interview that he left feeling an urgent need to respond further. “We had to keep our neighbors from dying on the street,” he said. “It made it very clear to me we needed a shift in leadership.”

At the time the Providence left was casting around for a way to build on its victories from 2023. Morales and other legislators, with the backing of Reclaim, spent two sessions pushing a package of legislation that they named a “tenant bill of rights.” At its core were just cause eviction protections, which prevent landlords from evicting tenants unless they have a qualifying reason. Two years in a row, the bills died in committee. “It was clear we’d hit a wall,” Denvir told me in a recent interview. “We had some power in the statehouse, and we had achieved everything we could with that power.”

But a new fight over housing was taking shape in the city council. The council president, Rachel Miller, had expressed support for the idea of a rent stabilization ordinance when she began her term in 2023, while Smiley, then the incoming mayor, had made clear that he opposed such a measure. In the summer of 2025 a special election for a city council seat in one of Providence’s toniest neighborhoods unexpectedly became a referendum on the issue; after an establishment candidate came out adamantly against rent stabilization, voters chose the only candidate who supported it (she also got a boost from a Reclaim endorsement and the organization’s help campaigning). In January Miller introduced the ordinance.

Rent stabilization became a new focal point for the debate about how the government should respond to the housing crisis. The proposal fiercely divided the city council, but a coalition of groups, including Reclaim, worked to secure a majority, and the measure passed in April. Polling showed 74 percent of likely Democratic voters in Providence supported it (only 59 percent of households rent in the city). Yet Smiley vetoed the law as promised. He said in our interview that he “did it on principle because it’s wrong for the city,” and that “sometimes you have to do what’s right, even if it’s unpopular.” That decision made David Morales the rent stabilization candidate. Morales’s campaign was already focused on the cost-of-living crisis, but after the veto he began to more explicitly cast the mayor as the pro-developer, anti-tenant choice. “That was the evidence that we needed to solidify to our neighbors that the city mayor is not on the side of working people,” Morales said. It showed, he told me, that “we had a mayor that was more susceptible to corporate interests than he was paying attention to the needs of our community.” 

The rent stabilization fight also fueled a number of other primary races in the city and the state—especially after the council failed by a single vote to overturn the mayor’s veto. To left-wing groups that had scrambled for a supermajority, the city councilor who decided their defeat was John Goncalves, who represents Ward 1, which encompasses much of the Brown University campus, all of downtown, and the mostly residential neighborhood of Fox Point. That neighborhood, which was once the heart of Rhode Island’s Cape Verdean community before a highway redevelopment project displaced many residents, has among the highest density of renters in the city, many of whom are college or graduate students. Campaign finance records show that Goncalves received large political donations from real estate developers and the landlord lobby in Rhode Island. The day of the vote, he sent a clear message when he neglected to show up in the council chambers.

In June Miguel Martinez Youngs, a policy staffer for the city council who was the principal author of the rent stabilization ordinance, quit his job to primary Goncalves. (Prior to working for the council, Youngs was first the organizing director and then a cochair of Reclaim.) Over the course of the campaign, Goncalves spent over $140,000 dollars—believed to be the most any city council candidate has ever spent on a race in Rhode Island. Youngs spent just over $20,000, and drew for his field operation on the coalition of progressive political organizations and volunteers that had also coalesced behind the Morales campaign. He ran on a clear message: he was the guy who wrote the ordinance, and he was challenging the guy who ensured it never became law.

In electing Youngs and his allies, many Providence residents seemed to be consciously voting for their own interests as renters. To Reclaim, this was a clear vindication of its strategy. After its first two tenant union campaigns dissolved into slow legal processes, the group raised money to hire full-time organizers, including a former union staffer from the militant SEIU 1199 New England who brought his experience with labor to housing. The group with which Morales celebrated his twenty-eighth birthday, the Charles Place Tenant Union, is one of four supermajority tenant unions that Reclaim has helped organize in the past year, all of which are in the process of collectively bargaining leases with their landlords; Reclaim envisions them as the first chapters in its project to build a statewide Rhode Island Tenants Union.

In the meantime, these unions may have tipped the scales in one of the fall’s closest city council races. Justin Roias, who had worked to turn the council chambers into a makeshift shelter that cold January night, and who has supported the tenant organizing efforts in his ward, faced a primary challenge from a pro-business centrist. On election day, the ward saw a 30 percent increase in voter turnout. Denvir of Reclaim suggested that formerly disaffected, now organized tenants may have been inspired to take part in the political process. Roias won by fifty-five votes.

At an election night party for the entire leftist slate on September 9, hundreds of people gathered in the courtyard of one of the repurposed mill buildings in Providence’s West End. The local brass band that often punctuates progressive gatherings in the city set the tone. Surrounded by the remnants of a long-gone industrial economy, campaign volunteers, local politicians, and the grassroots groups that carried Morales and his allies to victory gathered under a common vision for what the city could become. One after another, the candidates took the stage. Morales climbed the steps to chants of “David! David! David!” (Few people call him by his last name.) “Solidarity was on the ballot!” he proclaimed. “We chose to believe. We chose hope over fear.”

Also on the ballot: a movement that has swept leftists into city government in a growing number of places across the country—not just New York but Seattle, Ann Arbor, and Washington, D.C. As they take office, their challenge will be to deliver on a mandate for transformative change while facing down material constraints, especially fiscal ones. As Piper French wrote in a recent article about New York City DSA and the Mamdani administration in The Drift, “The terrifyingly high-stakes reward is the chance to make these intellectual questions material—to determine, together and apart, precisely what different could look like.”

The young Mamdani administration suggests just how complicated that task can be, as it tangles simultaneously with a federal government sending ICE agents into the city and a leftist base incensed by the NYPD’s collaboration with them—all while launching a 2-K program and filling more than 200,000 potholes. But unlike other socialist mayors, Morales will be working with a legislative branch that largely shares his vision for the city. A month after the primary, the Providence City Council threw its support behind the socialist Miguel Sanchez to serve as the next council president come January.

The Democratic establishment has yet to articulate a clear response to this wave of challengers. But the results in Providence show that a vague appeal to affordability falls short when twelve million tenant households in the United States spend more than 50 percent of their monthly income on housing. None of the candidates denied that the city and the state face a crisis. Yet as Morales’s campaign manager Ben Shanahan said in an interview, many establishment leaders still “refuse to actually commit to any material, immediate relief for people who really need it.”

Morales has vowed to sign a rent stabilization ordinance within his first one hundred days in office. He plans to establish a public developer at the municipal level, and to expand the city’s capacity to hold landlords accountable for unsafe living conditions. Smiley, meanwhile, has declined to endorse Morales in the general election. A few days after the primary, the outgoing mayor advertised a rental unit he owns at $5,500 a month—a 47 percent increase since 2020.

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
On March 29, 1985, Elie Hallak, a fifty-eight-year-old physician and the vice president of Lebanon’s Jewish Communal Council (Conseil communal israélite libanais), was abducted from his home in West Beirut. His kidnappers belonged to a shadowy militant Shiite network, associated with the milieu from which Hezbollah was then emerging, which called itself the Organization of the Oppressed on Earth. During his captivity Hallak was held alongside the journalist Jean-Paul Kauffmann and the sociologist Michel Seurat, who were abducted together on May 22 after arriving on the same flight from Paris, in a kidnapping claimed by Islamic Jihad. Seurat, a researcher at the social-sciences institute CERMOC (Centre d’études et de recherches sur le Moyen-Orient contemporain) who had lived in Lebanon for about a decade, was returning to Beirut; Kauffmann had arrived as a correspondent for L’Événement du jeudi. In a 1988 essay for that magazine, Kauffmann remembered that Hallak, unlike the other prisoners, was sometimes allowed to move without a blindfold; the guards referred to him simply as the hakim—the doctor.

According to Kauffmann’s later account, by December 1985 Seurat’s health began to deteriorate rapidly, and Hallak was brought to see him for brief visits each day. (In at least one case he remained by Seurat’s side as explosions shook the building.) Hallak asked that blood tests be performed and continued to treat Seurat even as the results came back incomplete or useless. Kauffmann compared him to Dr. Rieux in Camus’s The Plague: the physician who knows that he may be powerless against the disease before him and nevertheless continues to do his work.

Leading Christian and Muslim officials in Lebanon condemned the kidnapping, including Nabih Berri, then both the country’s justice minister and the leader of the Shiite Amal movement. When we spoke in August, Hallak’s son André told me that Imad Mughniyeh—then a rising figure in the militant networks later associated with Hezbollah—telephoned his mother, Rachel, to say that he wanted to secure her husband’s release because the hakim had once saved his own son from a serious illness. According to André, however, Hallak refused to be released alone. The following February the Organization of the Oppressed on Earth announced that it had executed Hallak, accusing him of spying for Israel. Rachel rejected that accusation.

Hallak was one of at least eleven Lebanese Jews—several of them members or officers of the Jewish Communal Council—abducted in the mid-1980s in operations attributed to the Organization of the Oppressed on Earth. Ten are believed to have died or been killed, with announcements of executions continuing into 1987. The fate of the eleventh, Salim Mourad Jammous, secretary-general of the Jewish Communal Council, remains unknown. The abductions began nine years into Lebanon’s civil war and two years after Israel’s invasion of the country, a major catalyst for Hezbollah’s emergence in the early 1980s.1 The remains of at least six, including Hallak, have never been recovered.

These abductions were part of a much larger Lebanese tragedy. During the civil war, between 1975 and 1990, some 17,000 people of different nationalities, religions, and political affiliations vanished. Most of them were civilians. Scores of others disappeared after the war, in the period of Syria’s domination over Lebanon. Among them were Lebanese citizens and stateless Palestinians seized by Syrian intelligence, sometimes with the participation of Lebanese security forces, and transferred to Syrian prisons, where many were held incommunicado and some were tortured.

The Lebanese state never produced a comprehensive accounting of the missing, and for decades families were left without any official way of confirming their fate. In 2015 the International Committee of the Red Cross began collecting biological reference samples from relatives of the disappeared, but as of 2019 this program had reached families representing only about seven hundred missing people—a tiny fraction of the thousands who remained unaccounted for. According to André, he and his siblings were never approached to provide DNA samples that might help identify their father’s remains. For decades the disappearance of Lebanon’s Jewish communal leaders received little sustained public attention. That changed this year, when their fate and the location of their remains emerged as an issue in the US-mediated negotiations between Lebanon and Israel.

US-led diplomacy began after Israel and Hezbollah returned to all-out war in early March 2026. In April Israel and Lebanon entered direct US-sponsored negotiations aimed at ending the conflict and addressing a broader set of security and political issues. Those talks, which had proceeded through seven rounds by early August before a planned eighth round was postponed, came to encompass Israeli withdrawal from Lebanese territory, the deployment of the Lebanese army in the south, and the disarmament of Hezbollah. On June 26 the negotiations produced a framework agreement under which the Lebanese army would take control of designated “pilot zones,” non-state armed groups would be disarmed there, and Israeli forces would withdraw progressively as those arrangements were implemented. Hezbollah, which was not a party to the agreement, rejected the framework and refused to lay down its arms while Israeli forces remained in the country. Israel has meanwhile continued to bomb Lebanon, destroying villages, detaining combatants and civilians alike, and devastating lives, ecologies, and livelihoods, while consolidating an occupation zone across a substantial swath of the country’s south.

Advertisement

One of the major questions in the talks has been the release of detainees and the recovery of missing persons and remains. At one of those talks in Rome in August, according to reporting by the pan-Arab daily Asharq al-Awsat, the Lebanese delegation submitted an updated list of thirty-four Lebanese detainees whose release it was seeking from Israel; by September 22 the Lebanese Association of Prisoners and Liberated Detainees said that it had confirmed thirty-nine Lebanese detainees in Israeli custody, while acknowledging that the actual number remained unknown. Three of those on the earlier list dated from previous periods of conflict—1978, 1981, and 2005—while the others had largely been detained since October 2024, including during the renewed fighting of March 2026.

Israel has not provided Lebanon with a comprehensive list of the prisoners it holds, and according to the Beirut daily An-Nahar it has refused either to let the International Committee of the Red Cross visit the Lebanese detainees or to provide ICRC officials with their names. (The ICRC has in fact been denied access to detainees held in Israeli detention facilities generally since October 2023.) It has, meanwhile, gone to extreme lengths to recover its own missing dead. In March 2026 Israeli special forces entered Nabi Chit in the Bekaa Valley under heavy air cover and desecrated the Al-Chokr family cemetery while searching for the remains of Ron Arad, the Israeli Air Force navigator who disappeared after ejecting from his damaged aircraft over Lebanon in 1986. Lebanese reports said the commandos excavated and opened a family grave; Israel subsequently said that no evidence relating to Arad had been found.2

It was hardly unexpected, then, that in recent rounds of negotiations Israel linked progress on the release of Lebanese detainees to information about Arad and possibly the recovery of his remains. And yet it also, more unexpectedly, tied movement on the detainee issue to Lebanese efforts to locate the remains of Lebanese Jewish communal figures and others abducted and killed during the civil war. In early September, through US mediation, Israel released five civilian detainees, three Lebanese and two Syrians—none of whom appeared on the list of detainees previously circulated by the Lebanese Association of Prisoners and Liberated Detainees. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s office said that the release followed “significant activity” by both Lebanon and Israel to locate the remains of Lebanese Jewish communal figures abducted and murdered in the 1980s, including unspecified “operations on the ground.” Israeli and Lebanese reports have since referred to maps, photographs, and the location of possible burial sites supplied to Lebanese authorities, although neither government has publicly identified who conducted the searches or precisely where they took place. The US State Department described the arrangement more plainly: “Israel is releasing detainees and Lebanon is helping Israel recover the lost remains of Lebanese Jews.”

All this has forced the issue of Lebanon’s disappeared Jews back onto the agenda of a state that has largely ignored it for decades. A September 5 report in the Beirut daily Ad-Diyar suggested just how much relevant material may have remained scattered within Lebanese institutions. Citing diplomatic sources, Ad-Diyar reported that officials had begun assembling a dossier of intelligence records and testimony from the period, and had provided American officials with documents and photographs as well as information about possible burial sites. The report does not prove that Lebanese authorities knew where the missing were buried, still less that they deliberately concealed that knowledge. It does, however, raise uncomfortable questions: How much information had been left languishing in the archives of a state that showed little urgency in accounting for its missing citizens, and why did that information acquire political value only when another state made those citizens’ remains part of a negotiation?

That choice by Israel exposed the Lebanese state’s failure toward these victims and their families, but it was far from a neutral humanitarian gesture. By conditioning the release of Lebanese detainees on Lebanon’s cooperation in locating these remains, Israel assumed a political standing in relation to the civil war’s Lebanese Jewish victims that resembled the standing it exercises on behalf of its own missing citizens. When the Associated Press correspondent Bassem Mroue recently asked Doron Spielman, a spokesperson for Netanyahu, to clarify why the recovery of Lebanese Jewish remains had become an Israeli negotiating interest, he answered that “Israel, as the nation-state of the Jewish people, has a profound and enduring responsibility to Jews throughout the world.” That responsibility, Spielman continued, “does not end at Israel’s borders, nor does it end with death.” 

Advertisement

The implications of this logic are troubling. It detaches Lebanese Jews, living and dead, from Lebanon’s own history and turns Jewishness itself from a diasporic identity rooted in many languages, places, and communities into a presumptive basis for political belonging to Israel. There is an unsettling historical symmetry here. The militants who abducted Lebanon’s Jewish leaders in the 1980s also treated their Jewishness as evidence of a political relationship to Israel, tying their fate to the demand that Israel withdraw from Lebanon and release Lebanese prisoners. Hallak and the other victims were Lebanese civilians who had remained in the country through the civil war, yet to their captors they were proxies for a state of which they were not citizens. In February 1986 the Organization of the Oppressed on Earth claimed that it had killed Hallak in retaliation for Israeli military operations in southern Lebanon; later that year it likewise said that three other Lebanese Jewish hostages had been executed in response to Israeli attacks.

Israel now appears to be making a similar conflation from the opposite direction. In this sense the current negotiations reach beyond the fate of the missing themselves, to the tension between Israeli ethnonationalism and diasporic Judaism, and by implication to the challenge posed by the Lebanese model itself: the possibility, however fraught and imperfect, that religious difference need not mean territorial separation and monoethnic national identities.

Beirut has a longstanding place in the Jewish history of Roman Phoenicia. By late antiquity it was home to an established Jewish community, with a synagogue that stood there until it was destroyed in the earthquake of 502 CE.3 In the twelfth century Benjamin of Tudela wrote about his encounters with Jewish communities in Beirut, Sidon, and Tyre, where Jews included Talmudic scholars, shipowners, merchants, and glassmakers whose wares circulated far beyond the city.

The first recorded burial in Beirut’s current Jewish cemetery, in Ras al-Nabaa, was that of Rabbi Moise Yedid Levy in 1829. Beirut’s Jewish community expanded rapidly over the nineteenth century, becoming part of the city’s commercial and civic life. In 1824 the Jewish traveler David d’Beth Hillel found some fifteen Jewish merchant families in Beirut, “natives of the country” who spoke Arabic and maintained a small synagogue; by 1856 another visitor counted about five hundred Sephardi Jews, many working as merchants and porters. After World War I the Maghen Abraham synagogue became the religious and institutional heart of a flourishing Beirut Jewish community. Most of the city’s Jews were middle-class and engaged in commerce; as Beirut expanded they increasingly lived beyond Wadi Abu Jamil, although the old Jewish quarter remained the symbolic and communal center of Jewish life.4

The Jewish cemetery in Sidon is even older than the one in Beirut. It lies on an ancient dune, in the fine sand that fed Sidon’s celebrated glassmaking tradition. (The Homeric epics already associate Sidon with exceptional craftsmanship.) Some of its tombstones are fashioned from fragments of ancient Greek and Roman columns, though many of the inscriptions are now illegible, as I learned when I worked on the cemetery’s restoration.

Jews historically lived not only in Beirut and Sidon but also in Tripoli, the Chouf, Aley, Deir al-Qamar, and elsewhere in the country. Aley and Bhamdoun, once popular summer resorts for Beirut’s Jewish community, still have historic synagogues that sit abandoned among mosques and churches. By the twentieth century Lebanon’s Jews sustained a dense network of institutions: Talmud Torah and Alliance schools, charitable associations, synagogues, batei midrash, businesses, and other social organizations. Tomer Levi has described this as the emergence of a distinctly “Levantine” Jewish community, formed through migration, commerce, and the plural social world of the late Ottoman port city.5

When Lebanon gained independence in 1943, its Jewish citizens remained part of the country’s constitutional and confessional order. Judaism was a legally recognized religion, its adherents protected by constitutional guarantees of freedom of conscience and communal rights in matters of family and personal status. The National Pact of 1943—the country’s unwritten political compact between President Bechara al-Khouri and Prime Minister Riad al-Solh—privileged the larger Christian and Muslim communities in the distribution of political office, but it did not render Lebanese Jews foreign to the state.

Even before independence, Alfred Naccache, Lebanon’s president under the French Mandate from 1941 to 1943, had publicly affirmed the place of Jews within Lebanese national life. During a visit to Beirut’s Maghen Abraham Synagogue, he praised their contribution to Lebanon and, according to the Jewish Telegraphic Agency, said that Jewish citizens would be given “a full share in the responsibilities of government.” The modern Lebanese state continues formally to recognize Judaism, even though the community today is numerically tiny.

As the historian Kirsten Schulze shows in The Jews of Lebanon: Between Coexistence and Conflict, Lebanese Jewish life did not end with the establishment of Israel in 1948.6 While most of Sidon’s Jews temporarily fled the city amid the arrival of Palestinian refugees and the movement of Lebanese troops toward the border, she writes, the Lebanese government “protected their property and restored it to the Jews upon their return.” In Beirut, too, the state deployed security forces to protect the Jewish quarter during periods of regional conflict. Lebanon thus differed markedly from Iraq and Egypt, where the 1950s brought denaturalization, expulsions, sequestration, and large-scale dispossession of Jews.

In fact, Lebanon was the only Arab country whose Jewish population increased after 1948. Part of that growth came from Syrian and Iraqi Jewish refugees who settled in Beirut. By 1951, Schulze estimates, some nine thousand Jews were living in Lebanon, nearly seven thousand of them Lebanese citizens. They generally, she observes, did not take the so-called Arab-Israeli war “to directly affect them,” because “they saw themselves clearly as Lebanese nationals—so much so that there were Jewish soldiers in the Lebanese army fighting in the war of 1948.” Their relations with Zionism were particularly revealing. The community was marked by “ardent Lebanese nationalism” and, among the majority, considerable “apathy towards the Zionist project,” Schulze writes, even as a small number of leaders and activists maintained close ties with the Yishuv. Schulze paraphrases Joseph Attie, the president of the council, who summed up the prevailing position in 1952: while some may have been sympathetic toward Israel, “their first loyalty was to Lebanon.”

The unraveling began after the 1967 Six-Day War, which Lebanon largely sat out, and accelerated with the growth of the Palestinian armed presence in Lebanon and the start of the civil war. Notably, in 1967 the Lebanese state still moved to protect the Jewish quarter during demonstrations. By the 1970s, however, insecurity had deepened; a bomb exploded at the Selim Tarrab Talmud Torah school, and the community’s numbers fell sharply as Jews, like many other Lebanese, began to leave the country. The Israeli invasion of Lebanon in 1982 marked a still more dangerous turn. Israel opened its border to Lebanese Jews and even offered them citizenship, but according to Schulze none were reported to have taken up the offer; many still described Lebanon as home. Yet from 1982 onward some Islamist militias increasingly associated Lebanon’s Jews with Israel; after the Israeli withdrawal from Beirut, that identification became deadly.

Such suspicions were not unique to Lebanon’s Jews. Lebanese political life had long been shaped by the external affiliations of its confessional communities—Maronites with France, Sunnis with Saudi Arabia, and Shiites with Iran. What distinguished the Jewish case was the ease with which religion could be made to stand in for nationality: to be Jewish was increasingly to risk being treated as politically Israeli. The consequences were not confined to the later kidnappings. During the civil war Jewish homes and institutions in Wadi Abu Jamil were damaged or abandoned; ironically, the Maghen Abraham synagogue itself was struck by Israeli shelling in 1982, forcing elderly Jewish residents to flee the quarter. By 1978 estimates of the remaining Jewish population ranged from about 450 to 1,000, down from roughly five to six thousand only a few years earlier; by 1980, according to estimates Schulze cites, only two or three hundred Jews remained in the country.

The point of narrating this history is not to romanticize Lebanon, or to deny the harassment and insecurity that made Jews there increasingly vulnerable. The civil war—profoundly shaped by the Palestinian Nakba and exodus, and later the armed Palestinian presence and its Lebanese alliances—shattered the country in which that life had been possible.7 Yet for many Lebanese Jews, departure did not represent a belated discovery of where they had truly belonged all along. The testimonies collected by the journalist Nada Abdelsamad in Wadi Abu Jamil, her 2009 book about the neighborhood, are striking in this respect: her interviewees consistently describe departure not as a homecoming but as an exile.8

Some went to Israel, but many settled in Europe, the United States, Canada, Latin America, and elsewhere, as did Lebanese of other creeds. For these exiles Lebanon was not merely the place they had escaped but a lost homeland to which they continued to return—in memory, in ritual, in friendship, and sometimes in person. Many Lebanese Jews in the diaspora have maintained a powerful attachment to the country, preserving a distinctly Lebanese identity through language, food, music, friendship, family memory, and religious practices.

As the Jewish population of Lebanon grew smaller, its physical infrastructure was left increasingly vulnerable. Under Lebanon’s confessional system, recognized religious communities have considerable autonomy over their communal institutions and property, including places of worship and cemeteries; for the dwindling Jewish community, maintaining that infrastructure became increasingly difficult. But some sites have been maintained or restored through initiatives involving Lebanese Jews at home and in the diaspora. The Jewish cemetery in Sidon underwent rehabilitation funded by a Lebanese Jewish expatriate, while the Maghen Abraham synagogue was extensively restored beginning in 2009 with support from the Lebanese Jewish community, diaspora donors, and Solidere, the private real-estate company created to oversee Beirut’s postwar reconstruction. The Sidon synagogue served for decades as a makeshift home for displaced families—first Palestinian and later Syrian—some of whom earned a little money by showing around curious visitors (myself included). According to Bassem El-Hout, the lawyer representing Lebanon’s Jewish community, the building has recently been vacated and restored to the community’s possession.

Does the State of Israel possess a special political claim over the Jews who worshipped there simply by virtue of their being Jews—wherever they lived, whatever citizenship they possessed, and whatever attachments they chose in life? The philosopher Michel Feher has considered this question in his latest book, Redevenir juif (“Becoming Jewish Again”), in which he seeks to reclaim a diasporic Jewish political identity against the presumption that Jewishness necessarily entails allegiance to the Israeli state.9 Feher is hardly the first to notice the affinity between one of antisemitism’s oldest fixations—the idea that Jews do not truly belong where they live—and the Zionist proposition that their authentic political home lies elsewhere. Theodor Herzl himself famously wrote in his diary in 1895 that “the anti-Semites will become our most dependable friends, the anti-Semitic countries our allies,” imagining opponents of Jewish presence in Europe as potential partners in Jewish emigration. Feher’s argument, however, goes further: Zionism does not merely find common cause with antisemites; it can reproduce something of the same logic by treating diaspora as a deficient or provisional condition and Jewish political belonging as properly located elsewhere. It is in this sense that he provocatively, but not illogically, describes Israel as “the least Jewish country in the world.”

The historian Avi Shlaim and the cultural theorist Ella Shohat have made related arguments about the experience of Arab Jewry. Shlaim recovers what it meant, historically, for people like him and his Iraqi family to inhabit the hyphenated category of the “Arab-Jew.” Shohat asks how that conjunction came to appear contradictory in the first place, tracing how Zionist discourse produced a rupture between Arabness and Jewishness and recast Jews from Arab countries within the Israeli category of Mizrahim.10 In different registers, both show how forms of Arab-Jewish belonging that had once been ordinary came to appear anomalous or destined to disappear into Israel.

The transformation was not merely semantic. In Israel, Arabic—the language of many Jews from the Levant and North Africa—was increasingly stigmatized, while modern Hebrew became the dominant language of public and national life and immigrants from Arab societies were incorporated into Ashkenazi-dominated institutions. Shohat has described this as a process of “de-Arabization,” in which Jews from Arab countries were recast as diasporic populations returning to their proper homeland.11 Shlaim recounts the same rupture from within: his family left Baghdad as Iraqi Jews and arrived in Israel to discover that their language and culture marked them as socially and culturally inferior.12 The treatment of Lebanese Jewish remains in the current Lebanese-Israeli negotiations is a strange twenty-first-century echo of this history.

Once accepted, the presumption that Israel has a particular claim even over Jews in the diaspora does not necessarily stop at the recovery of the missing; it can extend as well to the dead whose place of burial was never in doubt. After the August negotiations, the Hezbollah-aligned Lebanese daily Al-Akhbar reported that Israel had proposed linking the release of Lebanese civilian detainees not only to the recovery of missing Jewish remains but also to the transfer to Israel of the remains buried in established Jewish cemeteries in Beirut and Sidon—a proposal that would, as the paper noted, call into question the very legitimacy of a historic Jewish presence in Lebanon. There was a certain irony in seeing this argument appear in a pro-Hezbollah paper, given the history of Shiite militant groups in the 1980s treating Lebanese Jews as proxies for Israel. The political logic behind the article was unclear, beyond its effect of weakening the legitimacy of a negotiation in which, the paper argued, Lebanon faced asymmetrical Israeli demands and little reciprocal movement.

Major Israeli news outlets quickly picked up the story, from Yedioth Ahronoth and the public broadcaster KAN to English-language outlets like The Jerusalem Post. None reported that they had independently corroborated the claim by Al-Akhbar, a newspaper many Lebanese readers treat with skepticism, and no subsequent developments have yet confirmed it. The idea itself, meanwhile, had already entered Israeli public discussion. A few weeks before the Rome negotiations, Walla, part of the Jerusalem Post media group, interviewed a Beirut-born Jewish man living in Haifa who called on the Israeli government, if it reached an agreement with Lebanon, to include a provision for transferring Jews buried there—including his sister—to cemeteries in Israel. “It’s not just me,” he said; Lebanese Jewish families still had parents and grandparents buried in the country.

But there is an obvious difference, of course, between a family asking to move the remains of a relative and a state incorporating such transfers into negotiations over detainees. The former is an act of private mourning; the latter risks converting Jewish ancestry into a basis for national jurisdiction over the dead. Lebanon’s Jews were not Israelis-in-waiting, estranged from their proper national home. They were Lebanese Jews, and Lebanon’s failure to protect them does not erase that history or amount to a transfer of their citizenship after death.

Lebanon’s constitution rests on a premise antithetical to Israel’s. For all its failures, the country’s political order is nevertheless based on an idea worth defending: that different religious communities can coexist without ceasing to be themselves. A Jew need not be Israeli any more than a Maronite need be French, a Sunni Saudi, a Shiite Iranian, or a Druze the citizen of a Druze state.

Israel’s appropriation of Judaism, by contrast, retains something of the fin-de-siècle imperial imagination: the idea that separate religious communities are also peoples destined for territorial political expression. That principle is not merely implicit in Zionist history. It has been repeatedly inscribed into Israeli state doctrine, most explicitly in the 2018 Basic Law concerning Israel as “the Nation State of the Jewish People,” which declares that the right of national self-determination in Israel is “exclusive to the Jewish people” and commits the state to Jewish immigration and the “ingathering of exiles.”

This vision of a Middle East composed of increasingly purified ethnoreligious territories cuts precisely against how the region was made. Its cities were built by communities whose affiliations overlapped rather than aligned: Arabic-speaking Jews in Beirut, Baghdad, Aleppo, and Alexandria; Armenians dispersed across Anatolia, Syria, and Lebanon; Greek Orthodox Christians tied simultaneously to local cities, ecclesiastical networks, and the wider Mediterranean; merchants, pilgrims, refugees, and laborers moving continually between ports such as Beirut, Sidon, Haifa, Alexandria, and Izmir. The region’s social worlds were never innocent of hierarchy or violence, but neither were they reducible to territorially bounded, homogeneous peoples.

The Lebanese Jewish dead belong to that history. Lebanon has an obligation to investigate the fate of the members of its Jewish community who disappeared during the civil war, just as it has an obligation toward the families of the thousands of other missing persons who have waited for decades to learn what became of them. When the civil war ended in 1990, the country’s leaders chose amnesty over reckoning. The following year, Parliament passed a sweeping law that pardoned most crimes committed during the conflict, allowing many of the militia leaders who had prosecuted the war to reenter public life as ministers, parliamentarians, and party chiefs. The settlement helped bring the fighting to an end, but it also institutionalized silence: there would be no comprehensive accounting of wartime crimes, no serious process for establishing responsibility, and little official effort to determine what happened to those who went missing.

But closure without truth is difficult, and reconciliation without accountability harder still. While Lebanon cannot restore the dead or undo the disappearances, it can establish what happened where evidence survives, identify remains and those responsible where possible, and acknowledge the failures that allowed thousands to vanish without account. The creation of the National Commission for the Missing and Forcibly Disappeared in 2018 was an important recognition of that obligation, but without sustained investigation even this risks becoming another form of postponement. A state that asks its citizens to forget what it has never seriously investigated cannot plausibly claim to have left its violence behind.

The disappearance of the country’s Jews stands as one of the starkest indictments of the state’s failure to protect its citizens and to account for the missing. Yet we should, at the same time, be wary of treating that failure as evidence that Lebanon’s Jewish community belonged somewhere else all along. They were Lebanese citizens who disappeared in Lebanon, and their disappearance belongs first of all to that country’s own unfinished history of violence and impunity. Their Jewishness should neither remove them from this national reckoning nor make their fate a matter for another state to claim.

entries.title: Elaine Blair on Lena Dunham, Sex, and Television
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
In this episode of Private Life, Elaine Blair joins Jarrett Earnest to talk about feminism, sexuality, and television. They discuss her essay “The Loves of Lena Dunham” (published in the June 7, 2012, issue of the Review) in light of Dunham’s memoir, Famesick (2026), as well as the reputation of her HBO show, Girls. Earnest and Blair also talk about her essay “Fighting for Her Life” (from the June 27, 2019 issue), about Andrea Dworkin; how feminist thinking has shifted in the last few decades; and how cultural criticism reflects changing attitudes.  

Elaine Blair is a writer and contributor to The New York Review of Books. She has written for Harper’s, The New York Times, and The Paris Review. Next week’s episode will be a recording of Blair’s “The Loves of Lena Dunham” read by the actress Ruby McCollister.

entries.title: Bernie Sanders’s Utopia Lab
entries.summary: Season 1, Episode 2 of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
The second episode of Endgame with Fintan O’Toole welcomes the poet and critic Dan Chiasson, whose recent Bernie for Burlington: The Rise of the People’s Politician is part intellectual biography, part memoir and paean to a region of the country where progressives have often gone to test out their visions for a better society. O’Toole and Chiasson talk about Bernie Sanders’s early embrace of public media, his commitment to labor, and his lifelong emphasis on the pursuit of happiness as a political goal.

Dan Chiasson has been writing for the Review since 2009, focusing initially on new poetry collections and quickly expanding to include subjects as various as Keith Richards and Richard Linklater and Lydia Davis and the future of the humanities. He is the author of five books of poems and two books of poetry criticism, in addition to his recent book on Bernie Sanders. He is the Lorraine C. Wang Professor of English at Wellesley.

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
This article is part of a regular series of conversations with the Review’s contributors; read past entries here and sign up for our email newsletter to get them delivered to your inbox each week.

In our October 22 issue, Lola Seaton reviews Jonathan Buckley’s latest novel, One Boat. “Buckley’s best fiction,” she writes, “is refreshingly free of self-regard: lovingly crafted but out of devotion to his characters rather than to exhibit his technical gifts.” This commitment to the lives of the people in his stories makes his books “alive right up to their edges,” and while that virtue “may be traditional, what the novel was built to do,” Seaton continues, “it can feel radical.”

There is something about this ethic that a critic should inhabit, as well—a craft of devotion rather than exhibition. Seaton is a prolific young critic in the UK who pays as sharp and close attention to the shifting politics of the left as she does to contemporary novels. In venues ranging from Harper’s to the London Review of Books to the Financial Times, she has written about new fiction, Joni Mitchell, and soccer. For the Review, she has also reviewed Sheila Heti and Megan Nolan, as well as covering the 2022 London heat wave. She is an associate editor at New Left Review and a contributing writer at The New Statesman.

This past week, I wrote to Seaton to ask her about close reading, switching off your critical voice (if you can), and how to be an editor who writes.

Lauren Kane: As a critic reading a novel, what is the first question you like to ask?

Lola Seaton: I suppose one question I am always asking is: What am I noticing? This may expose how gropingly intuitive my approach to criticism is, but I think I try not to come with a quiver of preformed questions aside from that. Of course, one is inevitably loaded with expectations and prejudices, but the ideal of letting the work teach you how to consider it, as the philosopher Stanely Cavell counseled, is a useful starting point.

“What I happen to notice” may sound like a flimsy basis for passing judgment, which in a sense it is. Criticism does involve an outrage of sorts, though it doesn’t feel outrageous when you’re in the throes of it because you have a method, “close reading,” by which you convert your measly impressions into authoritative claims. Kant argued that aesthetic judgments are both subjective and presumptively universal. You are working on the assumption that what you notice isn’t random, that what you notice is really there, and means something, is noteworthy.

It’s partly a matter of confidence in one’s ability to read. But what is it to read? I think that it is in part to read yourself, i.e., to be attuned to your reactions, to take them seriously, and then to try to account for them. You could say doing criticism is getting better at noticing what you notice. Then you work backward from the effects, seeking their causes—the formal features and decisions that produced them. This sounds strange: Where is the strangeness coming from? Et cetera. Over time you build trust in yourself as a kind of litmus paper.

One practical issue is that your initial reactions—what you first noticed—can be remote by the time you turn in the essay. Recently I was finishing a review when I came across a note about the pleasure I was taking in the book, scribbled down when I didn’t know I would be reviewing it. I went back to the review and restored some of the enthusiasm I had forgotten I’d felt.

I don’t feel confident about “reading” just anything—classical music or ice hockey or whatever. You see what you look at, John Berger said, but before some art forms you aren’t sure where to look. You can feel obtuse, resourceless, almost naked, as though you don’t know where to begin or lack the means to decipher your experience. But I do think a lot of this is to do with confidence, which one acquires through exposure and by learning the language of the art form and the language of its criticism.

How has your approach to novels when you are simply reading them changed since you began writing criticism?

Reviewing has shaped, or rather skewed, what I read, in ways I partly regret. It’s a pleasure to read systematically, through oeuvres, but it’s also narrowing: there is less time for classic literature and for reading desultorily. It’s so nice to pick up something random. The upside is discovery. It’s gratifying to feel your taste both expanding and becoming more defined.

As for the way I read, it must be true that you can’t easily “switch off.” I think Roland Barthes wrote somewhere that he had an “illness”: “I can see language.” You hope that on balance your reading is enriched by the self-reflexivity I mentioned—noticing what you notice. But I worry about the interference. Even though I do it all the time, I find reading to be a very complex activity, not straightforward at all.

Advertisement

But then again what would it be to switch off? I don’t think analysis and absorption, criticism and pleasure, is always a zero-sum game. Criticism can seem like an intrusive, cerebral activity but it is also quite natural, when we are moved or entertained or disturbed or repelled by a work of art, to want to articulate those feelings and clarify their sources. The art of receiving art, like the art of making it, seems deeply related to the need to discover what we share.

What does it mean for a critic to dislike a book? When you dislike a book but find it interesting intellectually, do you think it is worth writing about, and how do you balance those two things in your writing?

I don’t feel I’ve always got the balance right. That’s partly because of the contingencies of how a book review comes about. You might be assigned a book by an author you’ve never read, and, chuffed to be asked, you say yes before having set eyes on a galley. Then when the book disappoints, you’re committed; you have a duty to be honest. Sometimes as a result the target feels ill-chosen—one can end up attacking a minor perpetrator of a much more general crime.

Some mediocrity you just turn away from. Other kinds give you an itch. “Interesting failures” can make more rewarding subjects than unequivocal successes. I think feeling disappointed or frustrated is a fairly reliable indicator of good faith. If you are disappointed, you had hopes.

But there’s no getting around the fact that one might end up saying negative things in public about someone else’s work. If part of being a published writer is exposing oneself to criticism, then part of being a published critic is living with the knowledge of the personal hurt your criticism may cause. This isn’t nice, but it’s less bad—less existentially disheartening—than the spectacle of culture going uncriticized. That threatens to make it all meaningless. The scholar Colin Burrow, discussing Helen Vendler recently, described the goal of criticism as telling other people how good something is. That may be true in universities where the evaluative component is elided because the literature being discussed has been canonized. But Burrow is wrong; appreciation is only one mode, and arguably not the most important.

I tend to think ambivalence is a good position from which to write. If you’re ambivalent then you are curious about what you think, you may not know in advance where exactly you are going to land. Of course you are always battling baser urges: to entertain, to impress, to amuse, to be original. One tries to keep these foibles in check via the discipline of faithfulness to the object: Am I being accurate?

You are a writer but also an editor, for the New Left Review. How do you find that those two modes interact? Does facility in one help the other, or does the editorial impulse ever make it harder to write?

I think overall the ledger must be positive: the daily exposure to writing, constantly working with language, learning moves you can steal and traps you should avoid, exercising your structural muscles. In a sense editing is itself a form of criticism in that it too is premised on close, critical, constructive scrutiny. But being an editor probably makes writing first drafts harder, or at least slower. The activities bleed treacherously into each other—editing can involve rewriting, and writing, certainly in my case anyway, involves self-editing. I waste untold hours fussing over syntax and word choices in paragraphs that no one will read. But that’s the horrible, exciting thing about writing: how you say something changes, subtly but consequentially, what you are saying and what you can say next. This makes it difficult cleanly to separate writing from editing, blathering on from fine-tuning; the process forces increasing precision on you.

Writing ought to make you a more compassionate editor, and editing, hopefully, makes you a more gracious or suitably sheepish writer. Both activities are arduous, often fiendish, which you can forget when you are engrossed in one or the other. It’s good to be reminded, when you’re editing irritably, how difficult it can be to make sense on the page for any length of time. Equally, when I’m the one sending in a draft, I’m aware that I’m not only offering the great gift of all my hard work but imposing a burden, one that will require much collective exertion.

Advertisement

Writing is unpredictable and vulnerable, and being an editor can make it more humiliating when it goes poorly—you’re supposed to be a pro! Then again sometimes editing doesn’t go well either. A mug’s game, as the late Len Deighton said, giving up writing spy novels for fountain pen–engineering.

What are your favorite “classic” pieces of criticism, especially ones that you return to?

That I don’t have a personal canon to hand must mean that, to my shame (or not), I’m not really a bona fide criticism nerd. When I’m writing criticism I’m generally not reading much of it—too demoralizing to watch soaring ballet dancers when you’re toiling over a teddy-bear roll—and when I’m not writing criticism, I prioritize reading novels, desperate to stretch my legs. Perhaps more than particular pieces, I return to particular critics—Leo Robson, James Wood, Thomas Meaney, Janet Malcolm, Vivian Gornick, Martin Amis, to name a very motley few—as models of what can be done, but mostly for refreshment, to hear their voices, their tone, their vocabulary when your own feels cramped and dull, and a reminder, when you’re miserably lost and sick of your own monotonous, lumbering sound, that this is meant to be fun, sort of, and that you’re just a human trying to explain something to other humans.
